<!-- What is established about the project (the language, the library, the tree and its tools, the specification and the plan) as it stands now, grouped by area: each entry the fact, its source and its test. One line per entry under its permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.`, written only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`. `FACTS-history.md` holds each change's provenance and the line as it stood before. What an entry holds and how it is written: the `coordinator` skill, `references/record.md`. -->

# Facts on record

## Execution model

- F-7 **Walk and the compiled path share the parser and the phases, and only the compiled path runs the static type checker.** Walk switches the checker off, and no switch turns it on. So walk checks no static types of expressions: an ill-typed expression shows only when it runs, as a failed dispatch or as another run-time error, such as F-239's refusal of an `if` on a value that is not a `Boolean`. At load, walk refuses some ill-formed declarations: the `fortress-repo` skill's `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", lists them, with their evidence in F-29 (`comprises` clauses), F-142 (the Meet Rule for Functional Methods) and F-145 (uncovered abstract methods and `override`). The phases and where the two paths part: the skill's "How a program runs". Detail: `explorations/repo-internals.md`, "The two worlds".
- F-9 **`fortress typecheck` checks a program against the compiler's library, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`, so it is no oracle for walk programs.** `Shell.java` calls `useCompilerLibraries()` for the command (row 69). P-12 has walk run the checker on its own programs after the switch-over, and walk cannot do so as it stands: it runs with type checking and the Scala checker off, the Java checker is gone (`compiler/StaticChecker.java:228-229`), and it has no case for the `CoercionInvocation` nodes that the checker inserts, by reading (row 833).
- F-11 **The code generator boxes every number, and boxing is the main representational cost of microGPT-shaped array code.** So a compiled `RR64` loop holds no `dadd` or `dmul` (the `fortress-repo` skill, "The compiled runtime"). In Java models of microGPT's three kernels, boxed elements cost 6.3× (dot product), 6.5× (matrix product) and 2.6× (row lift) over `double[]`. No such kernel compiles yet: the compiler prelude has no array type (row 305), and the arrays reach the compiled path with the one library (P-37). In a hot compiled loop, escape analysis removes the temporary boxes, and one box per assignment to a mutable variable per iteration stays (F-301), as long as C2's inline depth reaches each box's constructor chain (F-302). Detail: `perf-probes/kernels/REPORT.md` sections 2 and 4; `perf-probes/helper-calls/REPORT.md` section 4.
- F-12 **On the compiled path, the scalar `RR64` loop `bench1t` ran in 0.74 s in one session's measurement; the loop still pays for its generator, for boxing and for a transaction check at each use of its accumulator.** `bench1t` is `for i <- seq(1#20000000) do acc := acc 0.9999999 + 0.0000001 end` on a `var acc: RR64`, with both literals written in the loop. The time is the median of three loop-only runs at one thread (`compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`, "The four timings"). Times taken in different sessions differ on this machine, so compare only times from one session. What the loop does, read in its bytecode (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` sections 4 and 5): the `seq` loop becomes the compiler prelude's `countedseqloop`, which runs the iterations in order by a recursive split over boxed indices, with a closure call per element; each value is boxed (F-11); and the accumulator is a volatile cell whose read and write each first call `BaseTask.inATransaction`, as for every mutable local (F-40, what a size costs at run time, whose sized loop pays the same check). Within the boxing and the cell, the report counts four allocations per iteration, an interface call to the native wrapper and the casts, the part that unboxed doubles and `double[]` would attack. No share of the 0.74 s is measured.
- F-17 **The bytecode cache can come up empty after a library order that reports exit 0.** Running the same commands again, one at a time, made the jars. The cause is not known. Check the five jars before a compiled run (the `fortress-repo` skill's `build-and-caches.md`, "The library order"). Detail: `perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` section 1.
- F-18 **On the compiled path, the class loader makes the class of a generic instantiation at its first use, by rewriting the template's bytecode with ASM, and the rewriting only renames, so it gives no instance a `double[]` field.** The class is `InstantiatingClassloader`; the `fortress-repo` skill's "The compiled runtime" gives the mechanism. A size is part of the made class's name, as in `pNatMeth$Box⟦3⟧`, the object `Box` at size 3 in the probe component `pNatMeth`. Inside the class, the size's descriptor is `RTTIsize.of("<n>")` (F-129). A field of the template's type `T`, `LT;`, becomes `LFRR64;` in `Box⟦FRR64⟧`, and `[D` is no class name, so stamping alone keeps every number boxed (F-11). The team's direction for unboxing builds on this class per instantiation (the plan in `compiler/optimization/Unbox.java`; the loader's empty "expando" stub, `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-172`), but a loader that stamps an `RR64` instance with a `double[]` field, way A4 of array decision A (P-85), does not exist and is unmeasured. Walk instantiates generics in its own evaluator, not by classes. Detail: `perf-probes/nat/java.md` section 1; `coordinator/array-design.md` section 2 (probe 1); `reviews/array-design-ways.md` section 3, way A4.
- F-19 **By the specification, the iterations of a `for` loop, the elements of a tuple, and the arguments of a call or an operator may run in parallel, and a program must assume that they do.** A `for` loop is sequential only if every generator is, as `seq(g)` or `sequential(g)` makes it. An implementation may also run them one after another (`evaluation/parallelism.tex:88-90`), so a program cannot count on parallel runs either. For the elements of a tuple and the operands of an operator, each path starts a task only where it judges it worth it: walk by `TupleTask.worthSpawning`, which also governs a call's arguments, and the code generator by `ParallelismAnalyzer`. Compiled, a function call's arguments run in order (`CodeGen.evalArg`). A `for` loop over a range without `seq` runs by splitting the range into `do … also do … end` blocks. Under walk, every such block is a task, and walk's library splits down to single elements (`Library/RangeInternals.fss`). Compiled, the first block runs in place, and each other block forks only where `BaseTask.forkIfProfitable` judges it worth it, as tuple elements do; the compiler prelude's `parloop` splits down to `FORTRESS_LOOP_CHUNK` elements, 1 by default. `FORTRESS_THREADS` sizes the pool of worker threads (the `fortress-repo` skill, "Parallelism and mutable state"). By grep, no program under `explorations/`, the model programs and the probes, writes `spawn`, which starts an explicit thread, or an `also do` block, so their parallelism comes only from loops, tuples and arguments. The revival's tests under `ProjectFortress/` write both. Source: `Specification/basic/expressions/for.tex:28-32`, `tuple-expr.tex:23-24`, `operator-app.tex:58-59`, `evaluation/parallelism.tex:50-80`.
- F-20 **Sizes, the `nat` and `int` static parameters, are values at run time; they check shapes, and no optimization uses them (F-40, what a size costs at run time).** The compiled checker checks them (F-67), and a sized program loads and runs compiled (F-129). Under walk, `Vector` and `Matrix` take their sizes from an array built at run time: `f[\nat s\](v: Vector[\RR64,s\])` takes `s` from `array[\RR64\](3)`, and overloads on `Vector` and `Matrix` dispatch by rank (row 214). The array-type syntax `T[n]` with a `nat` parameter does not unify with such an array, "Cannot unify … with ArrayType", where `T[3]` with a literal size does (row 23). Walk matches sizes at dispatch. A mismatch, such as a `DOT`, the library's inner product, of a 2×3 matrix by a 2×3 matrix, whose inner sizes differ, is a `ProgramError`, "Failed to find any matching overload", that no `catch` takes (row 254). Source: `Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:96`.
- F-21 **The February 2011 Working Draft's bare `Nothing`, one object for every `T`, is accepted on neither path: the grammar refuses its `excludes` clause, and without that clause `T` is undefined.** The declaration is `object Nothing extends Maybe[\T\] excludes Just[\T\] where {T extends Object}` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/convenience.tex:40`). Both paths stop at a syntax error at `excludes`, since an object has no `excludes` clause (measured: `reviews/spec-refused-examples.md`, E4). Without that clause, both report `T is undefined` at the `T` of the `extends` clause: a `where` clause on an object binds no type variable of its `extends` clause, as row 17 holds for a trait. Today's specification refuses the form in any case, by instantiation exclusion, and marks it "Not allowed" beside the parametric `Nothing[\T\]` that the interpreter's library writes (F-167). P-90 still calls the bare `Nothing` future work that waits for such `where` clauses, not tried before then. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-maybe/REPORT.md` section 5.
- F-22 **When a component's name differs from the api that it exports, neither path finds the component, for an exported function or variable alike.** The specification resolves an imported api to any component that exports it (`Specification/basic/components/overview.tex`). The tree looks only under the api's name, unless a user maps the api to its component by hand with `LinkShell`'s `alink` or `clink`. The linker's component repository looks this way (`Linker.whoIsImplementingMyAPI`), so `fortress link` and walk print "Could not find an implementation for API … on path" before any code is generated. The code generator names a reference to an exported declaration after the api, and the declaring class after the component. The link step rewrites such a reference to the component only when the repository names it, so files compiled one by one, without `fortress link`, die with `NoClassDefFoundError`. The missing step is the repository's: finding the component that exports the api. The report names two repairs, neither built: the repository could search the source path for that component, or the code generator could emit api-named forwarders, for which three comments in `CodeGen.java` leave a place. Walk and `fortress link` need the first. Workaround: name the api after its component. Gated by the expected failure `compiler_tests/XXXExportVarRungXLinked.test` (row 320). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-export-var/REPORT.md`, "The measurement that separates them".
- F-23 **A comment placed after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span and of the unambiguous name the parser derives from it.** The parser's `createSpan` trims back over spaces only, and a declaration that ends in `end` is unaffected (row 359). So a comment-only library edit can change the syntax tree, and a before-and-after comparison of parse trees or diagnostics maps positions back first. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/REPORT.md` section 6, D1.
- F-24 **Under `walk`, a native can raise a Fortress exception that a Fortress `catch` sees.** It throws a `FortressError` that holds the exception's object, as `Int.overflow()` does for `IntegerOverflow` (F-132; row 347, fixed). A native bound to a helper of `nativeHelpers/` raises the library's own exception where the helper raises a class of the compiled prelude, such as `fortress.CompilerBuiltin$DivisionByZero`, so `DIV`, `REM` and `MOD` by zero on `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64` raise `DivisionByZero` (F-299, F-306, F-308, F-312). Any other Java exception of a native becomes a `ProgramError`, which no `catch` takes. Gated by the `overflows(...)` assertions of `tests/IntSemanticsRungI.fss`, and for a helper by `tests/NativeHelperRaiseWalk.fss` and, for each of the five types, `tests/<type>DivisionByZeroWalk.fss` and `tests/<type>RemainderByZeroWalk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-int-semantics-walk/REPORT.md` section 4.1.
- F-25 **On the compiled path, the class loader loads each class under the JDK's class-loading lock, so the first load of an instantiation's class is safe on four threads at once.** `InstantiatingClassloader.loadClass` holds `getClassLoadingLock(name)` for the whole load, as the JDK's own `ClassLoader.loadClass` does. Without the lock, two threads that first loaded such classes at the same time could race, and the run died with a `NullPointerException` (row 417, fixed). The test `compiler_tests/FirstLoadThreadsRungG` calls the generic overload `f[\T\](v: Vt[\T\])` at eight instantiations, `Vt[\A1\]` to `Vt[\A8\]`, from a parallel `for` loop of 800 iterations. Observed: at four threads it failed 5 runs of 5 before the lock, and passed 5 of 5 after. It is one of the gate's atomic runs, which run each program at four threads (`gate.md`). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/REPORT.md` sections 1 (the runs) and 12 (why this lock).
- F-26 **Under walk, when one of two applicable declarations has static parameters of its own, the call chooses on their declared domains where exactly one lies inside the other, not by the order in which they are written.** It builds P-45, the choice among overloads by declared parameter types, under walk. A declaration has static parameters of its own if it is a generic function or constructor, or a functional method with static parameters in a trait or object without any. Its declared domain, walk's symbolic instance, is its parameter types with each type parameter standing for itself under its bounds. Where neither declared domain lies inside the other, where each lies inside the other, or where neither declaration has static parameters of its own, walk compares the domains of the instances that the call makes. So a functional method of a generic trait or object is compared on its instance, and a generic dotted method is chosen by F-253 (a generic method at a dotted call, also chosen on declared domains). If the chosen declaration is generic and its instance takes an argument only by a conversion, walk converts the argument and dispatches the converted arguments again, so the most specific declaration for the converted values runs. In two cases walk keeps the chosen instance, with no second dispatch: an overloaded dotted method, and a position whose conversion `Coercions.coercionFor` does not find, such as a tuple converted element by element. Two generic overloads whose static parameters agree in name, kind and bounds share one symbolic instance, even if their `where` clauses differ; no test or library declaration has such a pair (row 478). Gated by `tests/DispatchDeclaredDomain.fss` and `DispatchConvertedAgain.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-dispatch/REPORT.md` sections 5.1, 5.2 (the second dispatch) and 5.5 (the symbolic instance).
- F-27 **Walk's load check reads again two kinds of overload pair that its parameter-by-parameter check refuses, and accepts those that pass: a generic declaration beside a plain one, read on their declared domains, and two plain top-level functions, not methods, whose overlap other declarations cover through `comprises` clauses.** To test a cover, the check cuts the overlap of the two domains, position by position, into parts by the `comprises` clauses. Each combination of parts must lie inside the domain of one declaration without static parameters that lies below both. So several such declarations may together cover the overlap. A search that does not settle refuses. A generic declaration beside a plain one passes where one declared domain lies strictly inside the other and the inner one's return type lies below the outer one's. Where neither lies inside the other, the pair needs the same cover, or declared domains that exclude each other read whole (F-258, exclusion over the whole parameter type). Equal declared domains are refused. It builds under walk P-46, by which a conversion never changes which declaration runs when one already fits, and P-60, by which several declarations below both may cover a meet. Two generic declarations are read on their declared domains too (F-252: the No Duplicates, Return Type and Meet Rules, each over its own instances). Walk still refuses the valid example of the POPL 2019 paper on symmetric multiple dispatch (`research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md`, p. 11:13), a set of three generic declarations (row 539). Gated by `tests/ComprisesMeetWalk.fss` and `GenericBesidePlain*.fss`, among others. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-dispatch/REPORT.md` sections 5.3 (generic beside plain) and 5.4 (the cover).
- F-28 **Walk instantiates a generic declaration declared to return `Any`.** `MakeInferenceSpecific` treats `Any` as it treats a trait type (row 157, fixed). Its visitor has no case for 11 of the syntax tree's 18 concrete type classes, and of those only the dimension forms can be written as a return type. Gated by `tests/GenericReturningAny.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-dispatch/REPORT.md` section 3.
- F-29 **Under walk, the load check refuses a trait or object that extends a closed trait of the program's main component where the trait's `comprises` clause does not allow it.** A closed trait is one with a `comprises` clause. The check reads every trait and object of every component of the program, the library's included, as a possible extender. An extender is allowed in three cases: it lies below a listed type; it is a trait whose own `comprises` clause lists only types that are allowed in turn; or it is a generic trait that some trait or object extends, and each of those extenders lies below a listed type (`Specification/basic/traits.tex`, "Trait Declarations"). The check does not yet read a clause declared outside the main component, the library's among them (row 551), or an object expression's `extends` clause (row 597). Nor does it check that each listed type extends the trait at every instantiation (row 598). A check that read the library's clauses would refuse at load every program that imports the library's `Reflect` (row 595), and four team tests and two demos whose objects extend `Number` or `Exception` directly (row 596). Their repairs come before that check and are the curator's. Gated by `tests/ComprisesUnlistedExtender` and `ComprisesGenericChildUnlistedExtender`, refused at load, and by the `XXX` tests of rows 487 (a type of another component below a generic subtrait of a closed trait), 551, 597 and 598, which stay green while walk still loads their programs. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-load-check/REPORT.md` section 5.
- F-269 **Under walk, a program's declarations of a library operator name are checked against the library's only when the program declares two or more of that name, and only on a cold cache.** One such declaration is not checked. Two or more are checked with the library's declarations, and the check can refuse them beside the library's generic declarations, even where they are more specific than the library's. It refused C4's former pair of `MAX` between an `RR64` and an `Array[\RR64,I\]`, in both orders, which C4 dropped when F-119's scalar extension took its place (row 341). It refuses the `Matrix`-specialised elementwise `×` of `apl/mg/elemwise_nat_probe.fss` (F-155). Walk writes a component to its cache before it runs this check, and skips the check on a component that it reads back. So a refusal appears once, on a cold cache, and never again (row 342). The check runs only when walk analyses the library itself again: deleting the program's own cache entries does not bring it back (row 342). So a test that depends on this check must run from an empty cache. Detail: rows 341 and 342; `compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/REPORT.md` section 4, a gated run that met a warm cache.
- F-291 **With the bound `Any`, the compiled path compiles, loads and runs generics at tuple and arrow static arguments as it does with `extends Any` written; `()` fails whatever the bound (row 339), and so does a generic dotted method with one tuple-typed parameter (row 832).** Measured once: generic functions, objects and traits, dispatch to a generic arm and `typecase`, at a pair or an arrow, with the static argument written or inferred. The class loader made the same classes by name, and the program jars read the same under `javap`, as the same programs with `extends Any` written under the compile command's bound `Object`. So the switch to the bound `Any` costs the run time no work for these shapes; its test cost is F-292. Not run: the one library's own instantiations at tuples, tuples of three or more and nested ones, generic functional methods at a tuple, a native that receives a tuple. With `extends Object` written, they are refused, or pass unchecked where the static argument is written (row 470); the compile command's bound is `Any` (`Shell.java:372`). No gated test. Detail: `perf-probes/bound-any-compiled/REPORT.md`, "The shapes by setting" and "What the class loader makes".
- F-301 **On the compiled path a native helper is called through a generated wrapper over the box classes, and once the loop is hot C2 inlines the whole path, so the call costs nothing of its own.** A binding `builtinPrimitive("pkg.Class.method")` and a written `import java` alias call compile to the same bytes: an `invokestatic` of `native.pkg.Class.method`, a class the compiled path writes into `nativewrapper_cache/`, which unboxes each argument with `getValue`, calls the helper and boxes its result with `make`, a new box each time (`compiler/nativeInterface/FortressMethodAdapter.java:303-327`; `compiler/runtimeValues/FZZ32.java:22-24`). A functional method such as `ZZ32`'s `+` reaches the wrapper through the dispatcher, an interface call, the springboard and the trait's static body. C2 inlines all of these frames, the helper, `make` and the box's constructor chain; only C1's profiling code refuses the helper and the chain's deep frames. Escape analysis then removes every temporary box, a helper's result passed into another helper among them, and one box stays per assignment to a mutable variable per iteration: 16 bytes for a `ZZ32`, 24 for an `RR64`. The library's form and the prelude's allocate the same. Observed once on one small program, `perf-probes/helper-calls/HelperCalls.fss`, by `javap`, C2's inlining log and the bytes that JFR counted, with no timing, on a machine shared at a load of 20 to 25; no test checks it. Detail: `perf-probes/helper-calls/REPORT.md` sections 2 to 5.
- F-302 **In those loops C2 inlines down to depth 12 from the loop, against the 16 at which it stops by default, and a temporary box whose constructor chain passes the limit is no longer removed.** At JDK 25's default `MaxInlineLevel=15` a frame at depth d inlines when d is at most 16. The prelude's `+` reaches `Object.<init>` under its result's box at depth 12, a top-level binding at 10. With the limit lowered to 8, a loop of two nested helper calls rose from 33 to 96 bytes per iteration, since its temporaries' chains no longer inlined. So an operator called from more than 4 further inlined frames keeps its temporary boxes. By reading, the one library's `ZZ32` springboard chain is two classes longer than the prelude's, `ZZ32`, `AnyIntegral`, `Number`, `AnyAdditiveGroup`, `Object`, `Any` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:730`, `:677`, `:380`, `:356`) against `ZZ32`, `Number`, `Object`, `Any` (`LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:210`), since a springboard extends the springboard of its trait's first `extends` entry (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:5072-5080`). If `FZZ32` extends the one library's springboard after the switch-over, the margin is 2 frames; not measured, since nothing compiles against the one library yet. Observed once (F-301). Detail: `perf-probes/helper-calls/REPORT.md` sections 3 and 4.
## The checker and the one library

- F-32 **The compiled path cannot reuse walk's glue classes, the Java classes that 143 of the one library's 449 live native bindings still name.** A native binding is a library body `builtinPrimitive("…")`; its string names a glue class, which takes walk's boxed values, or a static helper of `nativeHelpers/`, over plain Java values, which both paths call (F-298; F-299 holds the 306 that name one). Matched against those helpers at `a1f8c4b8b`, before any binding moved, the 449 were: 154 whose operation the compiler's prelude already binds to a helper at the same owner and signature, so only the binding's string changes, to name that helper (P-58); 59 whose helper exists, but no binding names it under that name and signature, 23 of them under a name that the compiler's prelude gives to another helper, such as the 12 wrapping operators (row 348); 158 that need a new helper; and 78 that need more, 36 methods of native I/O objects and 42 with no compiled analogue. Of the 449, 29 are object `IntLiteral`'s (`FortressBuiltin.fss:486-563`), 4 among the 154 and 25 among the 158; none of them can move yet, since their helpers take and answer the compiled path's `IntLiteral`, which walk's values cannot be, and walk reaches no `IntLiteral` native while its numeral is an `Int` (P-76; row 578). Every program's output needs `Writer`'s natives, among the 36 I/O methods, since `println` writes through a native `Writer`. MicroGPT's `nanoTime` names a helper (F-314); it also needs `getProgramArgsPrim`, which `System` calls as it loads; and `NativeArray`. The last two have no compiled analogue. The 42 with no analogue: `NativeArray` waits for the array decision on how a float vector's `double[]` store goes (P-85), and `Thread`, `Reflect` and `printTaskTrace` are off microGPT's path. Detail: `perf-probes/prelude/natives-shape.md` section 2; `coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-23.md`, section 4, "The planner's probes", "On the new base" and "The count".
- F-34 **Under the switch-over's setting the code generator refuses 38 declarations of the fourteen components that the distance stage checks, in 10 kinds, all of them declarations that the checker passes.** The setting is the distance stage's (F-53): the checker's failures caught per declaration, and the bound `Any`. Measured once, on `dbf4825e0`'s code, by `compile-ladder/plan-25/probes/codegen.sh` with its 288 helper strings put back on their glue classes; before local functions compiled, the same probe gave 47 in 11 kinds. The kinds that F-315 removes (`Any` in an `extends` clause, `forbid` and the `test` modifier) and the local function (F-320) no longer occur. A declaration counted at its first wall, and no emitted class was run. Each kind left has a ledger row or a plan line, among them varargs (row 624), `asif` (row 818) and "Not in the trait table" (row 733), so after the switch-over the code generator still stands between the library and bytecode. On climb batch 21b's base (`aa5c67d48`) the dispatch generator refused none of `FortressLibrary`'s 178 overload sets. No test checks the 38, since the gate's distance stage runs no code generation. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-codegen-local-functions/REPORT.md`, "5. Programs run old against new; the measure"; `compile-ladder/rung-codegen-walls/REPORT.md`, "5. Programs run old against new, and the probes"; `reviews/phase3-exit/zero-audit.md`, "Part C. The debt carried into phase 4", item 4; `perf-probes/codegen-distance/REPORT.md`, sections 2 to 6.
- F-35 **The `FortressLibrary` api has 9 declarations with a dead size: a size parameter that occurs in none of the api declaration's parameter types or return type.** They are the three one-dimensional `subarray` methods, with `nat o`; the two-dimensional `subarray`, with `nat o0` and `nat o1`, and the three-dimensional one, with `nat o0` to `nat o2`; and the traits `Rank`, `Indexed1`, `Indexed2` and `Indexed3`, whose `nat n` occurs in no member's type but tells `Rank[\1\]` from `Rank[\2\]`, as `Rank1 extends Rank[\1\]` does (`FortressLibrary.fsi:1245`). The component's `subarray` bodies read their offsets as values. The api declarations check clean, since a size that reaches no type, name or value is no error (P-40). The census of 2026-09-21 found 25 and missed the three-dimensional `subarray`; the 17 vector and matrix operators have lost their sizes since (P-40). Where a component declares a function without the api's dead size, the export checker reports the api's declaration as missing, since it compares static-parameter lists by length, name and kind. Detail: `perf-probes/nat/REPORT.md` sections 2 (the 25, by line) and 7 (the export checker).
- F-36 **The code generator's `FnNameInfo.boundsFor` gives a size parameter a size argument, and every other kind a type argument.** A `bool`, `dim`, `unit` or `opr` parameter still gets a type argument, a latent defect; the checker refuses the first three by name (F-67). A size symbol stays in the mangled name and needs no descriptor. Only a literal size reaches the class loader, which takes its descriptor from `RTTIsize.of` (F-129). Detail: `perf-probes/nat/java.md` sections 1 to 3.
- F-37 **On the compiled path, a `typecase` clause on a sized type, such as `Vec[\ZZ32,3\]`, tests the value's own class, also when the size is a static parameter of the enclosing function.** The test is one `INSTANCEOF` on the class of the instantiation, `Vec⟦FZZ32,3⟧`. In a generic function, the class loader puts in the size when it makes the function's instance. So a `typecase` tells `Vec[\ZZ32,3\]` from `Vec[\ZZ32,4\]`, and does not read the descriptor that a size has (P-41). Limit: a `typecase` that is a whole function body, with clauses that need a coercion, fails in code generation, with a size or without (row 340). Gated by `compiler_tests/NatRtCase` and `NatRtCaseGen`; the bytecode was read in `perf-probes/nat/size-probes.md` section 4.

The checker's return-type rule compares the arms' own sizes (row 410). The dispatcher skips a size parameter's bound (`compiler/OverloadSet.java:1501-1502`). Gated by `compiler_tests/NatRtDisp`, `NatRtDispSize` and `NatRtDispTrait`. Detail: `perf-probes/nat/size-probes.md` section 2.
- F-39 **An operator static argument is a name substituted when the declaration is instantiated, on both paths and by the specification; no code reads it at run time.** An operator static parameter is declared `opr`, as in `object Op[\opr ODOT\]() end`. The specification and walk substitute the operator's name into the declaring trait's or object's methods. The compiled path carries it in the name of the instantiation's class; the operator has no descriptor, where a type or a size has one (P-41). No live declaration of the one library has an `opr` static parameter: `FortressLibrary`'s two, in `embiggen` and `Monoid`, are inside comments. In `tests/`, `compiler_tests/` and `other_compiler_tests/`, nine test files declare one. Compiled, `Op[\+\]()` dies with `NoSuchMethodError` on `Op❮+❯$RTTIc.factory()`, the factory of the instance's descriptor class, where walk prints `Op[\+\]` (row 366, open; its expected failure is `compiler_tests/XXXOprParamRungS`). A three-line change to `MethodInstantiater`, measured but not landed, fixes row 366's program run as a probe, `compile-ladder/rung-default-rendering/probes/skeptic/SkOprParam.fss`; the gated `XXXOprParamRungS` was not run with it (`perf-probes/nat/size-probes.md` section 5). Detail: `perf-probes/nat/opr-kind-history.md` sections 2 (the specification and both paths) and 3 (no reader at run time).
- F-40 **Measured on 2026-09-24 for two size designs that were not built, a size cost a few kilobytes at load and nothing in a hot loop, and only the overload dispatcher read a size off a value.** The two designs were design A, descriptor classes stamped for each size of each generic, and design B, a class for each number, passed to the generic's descriptor factory; both ran on the size probes' private build (`perf-probes/nat/size-cost.md` section 1). The built design, one descriptor object per size value from `RTTIsize.of` (F-129), is neither, and nobody has measured its load size or its loops. Under either design, a size's classes came to a few kilobytes, against the 8.6 MB of classes that every run loads. A loop bounded by the size constant was not measurably faster than one bounded by the storage's length read at run time. The loop cost about 31 ns per element, which the bytecode shows going to a transaction check on each read and write of a local, to boxing, and to a method call for each element read. Once C2 compiles a hot loop, a native helper's call is inlined whole and costs nothing, and the boxes of its mutable variables stay (F-301). A call dispatched on a size cost about 4 to 20 ns more than the same call that the checker resolved at compile time. The built design's rung measured only the dispatcher's lookup of a literal size's descriptor: 0.9 ns on the landed build, its six runs from -2.2 to 7.0 ns, and 2.6 ns on an earlier build, on a dispatched call of about 23 ns. By reading the code of 2026-09-24, no optimization uses a size (F-20 holds it for today's tree), and a dispatched call tests a size once per overload arm tried, as the built dispatcher's literal leaf also does (`OverloadSet.java`, `SizeLiteralStructure`). Detail: `size-cost.md`, "The answers"; `compile-ladder/rung-size-runtime/REPORT.md` section 12.
- F-41 **The compiled dispatcher tests a size that two parameters share, in `DOT`'s shape, for equality in both directions before it chooses the arm that shares it.** `compiler_tests/NatRtDot` declares `dot[\nat n\](a: Vec[\RR64,n\], b: Vec[\RR64,n\])` over a user object `Vec`, beside a catch-all `dot(a: Any, b: Any)`. Sizes 3 and 4 reach the catch-all: typed statically, in the one order that the test makes, and dispatched at run time, in both orders. Walk printed the same in the probe. A static mismatch compiles with no error: the checker gives it the catch-all's signature. The dispatcher's equality test is the team's own check for a type variable in two invariant positions (`OverloadSet.java`). The library's `DOT` was not run compiled; by reading, the matrix product's shared inner size takes the same check. Gated by `compiler_tests/NatRtDot`, which checks the four outputs. Detail: `perf-probes/nat/size-rung-probes.md` section 3.
- F-42 **The compiled checker skips a compilation unit's (an api's or a component's) overloading and return-type checks when an earlier stage of that unit has reported an error.** `StaticChecker` returns before `OverloadingChecker` if the earlier stages found errors (`StaticChecker.java:268-279`). So clearing an early error can raise the checker count, which sees only the errors before each unit's early return (F-53). The distance runs every stage of every unit whatever the earlier stages reported, so these errors are not hidden from it (`tools/distance/run.sh`, header). Detail: `perf-probes/nat/zero.md`, its opening section.
- F-43 **The overloading checker's memo hides some errors, and which ones changes from one build of the checker to another, so the gate's checker count and distance run with the memo off.** The memo keeps a "valid" verdict per pair of declarations. A pair that several traits inherit is checked once per trait, at that trait's instantiation, in hash-set order, so a pair valid for one trait is taken as valid for the next (`perf-probes/nat/triage.md` section 1). The memo is on by default (`OverloadingChecker.scala:79`), so an ordinary `fortress compile` can miss these errors. The JVM property `-Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=false` turns it off; the gate's checker count and distance stages set it.
- F-44 **The compiled checker enforces the multiple instantiation exclusion rule and relies on it, and the one library meets the rule.** The rule: no type extends two different instantiations of one generic trait. The checker's Return Type Rule relies on it: with the rule relaxed alone, a program passes the checker and dies with `IncompatibleClassChangeError` (`OverloadingOracle.scala:81-105`; the probe `ProbeMIEPick`). The team's JVM type mapping relies on it too: no closure of extends lists names one generic at two static arguments, so the class that template expansion makes for an instantiation carries the type relations over as Java ones (`Papers/Implementation/TypeMapping.tex:125`, read). F-48 gives the kinds of static argument that the rule compares. Walk applies no instantiation exclusion: it accepts a type that extends two instantiations, and its overloading check does not count them as excluding (row 416; the review's section 3). P-43 keeps the rule. Besides the flat number tower of P-43, the library meets it by three changes of `952892a00`: `TotalComparison` extends `Comparison` and `StandardMinMax[\TotalComparison\]`, no longer `StandardTotalOrder[\TotalComparison\]`; `AnyMaybe` extends `AnyUniqueItem` alone, no longer `Equality[\AnyMaybe\]` beside it; and `andCondCombine` chooses `andRelCond` by a `typecase`, in place of a second `ANDCOND`. So under walk, a program's `p1 ANDCOND p2` of two relational predicates, conditions built from a relation over a generator, which `filter` fuses, is no longer itself a relational predicate (row 458). The distance holds no exclusion error (F-53). Detail: `reviews/multiple-instantiation-exclusion.md` sections 1 to 3; `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:122-124`, `:981`; `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4897-4903`.
- F-45 **Without the exclusion rule, every dispatcher would have to call its generic arms at the call site's static arguments, and no published work resolves a value that is in two instantiations of one generic under run-time dispatch.** The loader already gives a generic dispatcher the call site's static arguments; without the rule, its arms would have to use them instead of arguments read from the value (`reviews/mie-probes/scope-call-site-dispatch.md` section 3). The call at the dispatcher's static arguments is built for template dispatchers (F-136), and, by reading, not for one with an `opr` or `nat` static parameter (`compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/REPORT.md` section 9). The team's 2012 patents allow a self-typed generic, one that comprises exactly its parameter, at several instantiations along a chain of subtypes: the forest rule (`reviews/mie-probes/patents-forest-rule.md` section 1). Alone, the forest rule leaves the specialisation hole open: a specialised declaration, more specific than the generic one, runs for a value at a narrower level of the chain, a subtype, and returns a type that a caller typed at that narrower level does not expect. Compiled under a shadow checker with the forest rule, a patched copy of the checker that never landed, such a run dies with `IncompatibleClassChangeError`; the tree's checker refuses such a program (the same note, section 3). Route C adds a return-type rule that closes the hole (F-46). Detail: `scope-call-site-dispatch.md` section 3; `reviews/mie-probes/literature.md`, "What the field settled and what it did not".
- F-46 **Route C, the patents' forest rule with a return-type rule over every level of a chain, closes the specialisation hole (F-45), but going back to a nested number tower under it needs work beyond the checker.** The library's tower was nested before route A flattened it (P-43). Built as a shadow checker on 2026-09-24 and run through the zero probe's stack on a library copy without the reduction markers, route C refuses 25 pairs at 21 of the nested tower's declarations: specialisations that a level below does not cover. Completing the tower needs seven more declarations and the identification of `Integral[\ZZ32\]` with `ZZ32`. The patents' `comprises T` on the self-typed traits licenses that identification, but it overflows the checker's stack (measured on the zero probe's copy of the checker, in the recursion of `Formula.scala` that the tree shares). A hierarchy check of its own could enforce the identification instead; none is built. Leaving route A for route C also needs: the tower nested again; the call-site fix in every dispatcher (F-136); in the code generator, a method for each middle level of a chain, whose absence, by the error text, makes such a chain die with `AbstractMethodError`; walk to accept the specialised pairs without overflowing on `comprises T`; and, for the identification, a way past the checker's overflow or the hierarchy check. Detail: `reviews/mie-probes/route-c-experiment.md` sections 2 to 5.
- F-47 **The exclusion rule refuses some of the specification's own examples; in their place, a parametric object with a factory, or a widening function, runs on both paths as a user program.** The refused examples are E1 to E10 of `reviews/spec-refused-examples.md`, "What was found": among them three `where`-clause examples, the Working Draft's `Nothing`, the nested number tower and `RationalQuantity`. The `where`-clause examples stop on both paths before the rule, in name resolution, at `T is undefined`. The alternatives were measured as user programs that declare their own types: a parametric object with a factory, such as `object Empty[\T\]` with `emptyList[\E\]()`, and a widening function, such as `widen[\T, S extends T\](c: C[\S\]): C[\T\]`. The library's `Nothing[\String\]` does not yet run on the compiled path's prelude (row 331, F-167). A marker object with a `coerce` in the generic trait, as `AltEmptyCoerce` has in `SList[\T\]`, also runs compiled, and walk applies such a coercion (row 389). The 2012 `covariant` keyword passes the compiled checker and dies at run time (row 404). The compiled checker refuses a coercion with its own static parameter between two instantiations, `coerce[\S extends T\](c: C[\S\])`, as a cyclic hierarchy. Inferred from the forest rule: route C (F-46) would rescue neither the `where`-clause examples, `Nothing` nor E8, the internal appendix's "Disjunctive Constraints"; only the tower (E5) and the root `Object`'s algebra (E7) would keep their original text under it. Detail: the same note.
- F-48 **The compiled checker's exclusion rule compares type arguments, and sizes only when both are literals.** Two boolean arguments count as no exclusion: `object F extends { Flag[\true\], Flag[\false\] }` passes the checker and dies in code generation (row 406, `compiler_tests/XXXBoolExtendsTwice`). Nor does a static parameter beside another argument: `object O[\nat n\] extends { Vec[\n\], Vec[\3\] }` passes the checker and dies at load with `ClassFormatError` (row 414, `XXXNatExtendsTwice`; the row also places its cause in `TypeHierarchyChecker`'s check of `extends` clauses). Two literal sizes do exclude: the checker refuses `object V extends { Vec[\3\], Vec[\4\] }`, "Types Vec[\3\] and Vec[\4\] exclude each other" (row 402, fixed). Gated by `compiler_tests/XXXNatExcludeChecker`, for the refusal of two literal sizes. The code is `TypeAnalyzer.scala:544-551`, "Todo: Handle bool args". Detail: `reviews/spec-refused-examples-judgement.md` section 6.
- F-49 **Under walk, a value form and a function form of one name are chosen by the argument's run-time type, so with the element type `Any` a function passed as the value goes to the function form.** Given a function, `fill` on an array of element type `Any` stored the function's results, `c[1] = 11`, not the function. The compiled checker refuses such a pair under the bound `Any`: a functional whose one parameter has a parametric type bounded by `Any` cannot be overloaded (the probe `FillBoxAny`). The one library has no such pair: `fill` takes a value and `tabulate` a function (F-158). Detail: `reviews/fill-overloads-ways.md` section 2.
- F-50 **The compiled checker lets overloads differ in static parameters, as the model of the OOPSLA 2011 paper does, which the specification now states (F-174); as ambiguous, it refuses only the pairs it cannot prove unambiguous.** It builds P-45. It cannot prove a pair over open traits, which no `excludes` or `comprises` clause closes, nor one whose domains exclude only through the exclusion rule and a bound, as the library's `CAP` on `ScalarRange[\I\]` beside `Range2D[\I,J\]` does. It also refuses some pairs that the paper accepts, by its Return Type Rule and by its positional rule, under which two generic declarations in the more-specific relation agree on their static parameters by position (F-75). Other gaps have their own owners: two generic arms on a bare type variable fail compiled (F-174, row 537); and walk runs an arm whose size the call leaves unfixed, with the size unbound, where the checker drops the arm or refuses the call (F-69, row 400). Detail: `reviews/overload-static-params-ways.md` sections 2 and 3.
- F-51 **A generic call converts a narrower argument for a parameter typed by a type variable that another argument fixes, on both paths.** For `scale[\T\](b: Box[\T\], x: T)` and `b: Box[\RR64\]`, `scale(b, 3)` takes `T = RR64` and converts the `3` (row 388, fixed). So under walk the library's array-scalar `+`, `-`, `MIN` and `MAX`, and the matrix-scalar juxtaposition and `DOT`, take a `ZZ32` scalar with `RR64` elements. F-73 and F-137 give each path's rule. Gated by `tests/InferCoercionRungK` and `compiler_tests/InferCoercionShapes`. Detail: `reviews/numeric-hierarchy-integration-review/row388-container-probe.md`.
- F-52 **Neither path can use `RationalQuantity` as the specification declares it: the advanced numbers chapter's rational type, refined by `bool` static parameters for its sign, infinities and NaN (`Specification/advanced-lib/numbers-advanced.tex`).** The team's `ProjectFortress/tests/conditionalExtension.fss` declares it as the chapter does: a trait that extends its own instantiations with weaker flags, under a `where` clause. The compiled checker refuses it, "Cyclic type hierarchy: Type RationalQuantity transitively extends itself". Walk runs that test only because nothing instantiates the trait; a probe that instantiates it fails under walk. Measured by the note's probes, which `84aef6a4f` removed (`reviews/flattening-questions-ways/Q3*.txt` in its parent). Detail: `reviews/flattening-questions-ways.md`, "Question 3", section 2.
- F-53 **At the last landed gate, climb batch 27's, the distance to the switch-over is 0 errors and the checker count is 0.** The distance counts the compiled checker's distinct errors over the interpreter's library, its twelve apis and their twelve components, running every stage of each whatever the earlier stages reported, and classes them by root cause (F-54). Since climb batch 22c the stage also checks `List`'s two imports, `CovariantCollection` and `OneShotFlag`, fourteen components in all (F-288). Climb batch 22 cleared its last five: the export error, where the `FortressLibrary` component differed from its api, by the api's lines (F-282, F-286), and four body errors, row 731's three sites and the fused arm of `__bigOperator2` (row 632), by library text (F-285). Row 731's checker gap stays open for user programs and the team demos (F-285). The checker count checks only the `FortressLibrary` component, with the apis it imports, and each unit stops at its first failing stage; the component's run now ends clean, which the stage reads as 0 (`tools/checker-count/run.sh`, since `36ec68cab`), and nothing crashes (F-233). A rise in either is reported and turns no gate red on its own; the count's stage can still turn the gate red on the faults that F-66 names, such as a crash that no rung listed (P-39). A rung measured by either takes the last landed gate's tables as its starting values: that batch's `compile-ladder/climb-batch-<N>/gate/distance.txt` and `checker-count.txt`, and the per-site list `compile-ladder/gate/distance-sites.tsv`, which holds the last landed gate's sites, none now (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "The checker count and the distance").
- F-54 **The gate classes the distance to the switch-over by root cause.** The `#class` rows of each gate's `distance.txt` hold the count of each class, such as X1 for an export error, BR for a big operator's body, and OT for the other body errors, one-off library slips and checker limits; `explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/classify.py` assigns them. F-53 gives the last gate's. That gate's `distance.txt` reads `#crash none`: the checker checks the `FortressLibrary` component to its end, `Array3`'s body included, without a crash (F-233). Detail: `perf-probes/prelude/distance-triage.md` section 2.
- F-55 **Static arguments are inferred with coercion on both paths: the compiled checker from the arguments' static types and the expected type, walk from their run-time types.** So a mixed-width call takes the narrowest type into which its arguments convert, as P-74 decides. F-73 gives the checker's rule and F-137 walk's; F-87 lists where the checker has an expected type. Under walk, a typed binding converts a call's result after the call and does not fix the call's static arguments: `a: BoxK[\ZZ64\] = wrapK(3)` infers `T` from `3` as `Int` and is refused, since no coercion converts a `BoxK[\Int\]` (row 510). A parameter with no written bound is bounded by `Any` on both paths, so a parameter that nothing fixes takes `Any` (F-78). Gated by `compiler_tests/InferCoercionShapes` and `tests/InferCoercionRungK`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-inference-checker/REPORT.md` section 3.2; `compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/REPORT.md` sections 2 and 9.
- F-56 **The compiled checker keeps the expected type, for inferring the call's static arguments, at a call written `f(x)`, which the parser builds as a tight juxtaposition: `f` and `(x)` with no space between.** It keeps it at a method call and an operator too; F-87 lists the other contexts. Only desugarings reach the `fnApp = true` path of `scala_src/typechecker/impls/Operators.scala:88-90`, so an edit of that path alone changes nothing for a call written `f(x)`. Gated by `compiler_tests/InferCoercionShapes`. Detail: `reviews/numerics-plan-coordinator/measure-D.md` section 1.
- F-57 **A numeral's type depends on the path and on the library in scope, and in generic code only the getters `x.zero` and `x.one` and the witness `typecase` give a `T` on both paths.** The witness `typecase` is a `typecase` over a function of type `() -> T`, with one clause for each number type (P-78). The checker types a numeral `IntLiteral` or `FloatLiteral` by its form, as the builtin library in scope declares those types (F-79). Walk types an integer numeral by its magnitude, as a `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `ZZ`, which it prints `Int`, `Long` and `BigNum`. In code generic over `T extends Integral[\T\]`, `x + 1` fails the checker but runs under walk: no coercion from a numeral into an arbitrary such `T` can be declared, since a generic coercion is refused as a cyclic hierarchy. A numeral bound to `NN32` or `NN64` fails under walk, and `1.5` bound to `RR32` fails on both paths (row 454). Neither path refuses an out-of-range numeral statically: the compiled run raises `Not in range for ZZ32` at run time, and walk refuses it when it runs, at the typed binding it does not fit (row 325). Walk also refuses, against the specification, a numeral beyond `ZZ32`'s range bound to `RR64`, which should hold the float (row 443). Detail: `perf-probes/prelude/distance-triage.md` section 2.3; `reviews/numerics-plan-coordinator/evidence-B.md` sections 3.1, 4.1 and 6.2, measured before the numeral switch (F-79); `x.zero` by reading, not measured.
- F-58 **When measured, on an earlier library, microGPT's flat program, C4, had 26 errors of its own under the compiled checker, and none came from a numeral's type.** 15 were arrays without sizes: `Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]` where the library wants `Vector`, `Matrix` or `Array3`. 5 were numeral powers such as `10.0^(-5)`, refused as ambiguous because two declarations of `^` each needed the integer converted (row 533). 6 were small slips. On a copy patched with decision D's diff, which sizes the model's arrays (P-87), 14 remained: the 5 powers, 3 `DOT` calls that failed on the api's unused sizes, 1 bridge, `adam`'s, that passes arrays sized only at run time, and 5 small slips. Since then the 17 vector and matrix operators' unused sizes are gone (F-35), so by reading the 3 `DOT` refusals are cleared. Since then too, `MultiplicativeRing`'s `^` takes an `AnyIntegral` exponent, and `RR64` declares `^(self, b:AnyIntegral)` beside its `^(self, b:Number)`, the component's header (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:285`, `:367-368`). The distance stage's driver checks a component of `10.0^(-5)` and `10.0^(-8)` against the interpreter's library with no error, so the tie row 533 names does not reproduce there. Each count is a floor, since the checker stops a block at its first failing statement (row 474). Detail: `reviews/array-design-ways.md` section 2; `compile-ladder/rung-integer-power/REPORT.md` section 7; `compile-ladder/rung-export-last/SKEPTIC.md` section 3.
- F-59 **`SUM` and `PROD` take their identity from the static argument, and the compiled checker needs that argument written in every clause form.** It builds P-78, with a witness `typecase`, a `typecase` over a `() -> T` function with one clause for each number type. The compiled checker takes the element type from neither the clauses nor a declared type that receives the value (row 731; P-78). So for a generic big operator whose bound names its parameter, such as `SUM`, `PROD`, `BIG MAX` and `BIG MIN`, an unwritten static argument has no instance at its bound, and the call is refused. A plain-bounded big operator takes its bound, or the reduction's expected type where the bound does not fit (F-221). Walk runs such a call: it instantiates the big operator at its value's declared type, else at its elements' join, and leaves the parameter open only with neither (F-228, F-143). C4 writes the static argument, as the team's tests do: `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#i] matCount(j)`; so does the interpreter's library at its own sites (F-285). `SUM e` over a collection `e`, and `x DOT y`, need none (P-78). Gated, for the witness and a plain bound, by `compiler_tests/WitnessIdentityRungG` and `InferBigOperatorUnwritten`; the refusal is row 731's, and no test pins it. Detail: `reviews/sum-replacement-judgement.md` section 5, Table 2, measured before P-48; row 731 gives today's mechanism.
- F-60 **The coercions between number types carry a sum's zero and a product's one into every wider type by themselves, but not a maximum's identity.** A coercion keeps the arithmetic, on both paths. A maximum's identity is its type's least element, which a coercion does not carry; `ZZ` and `QQ` have none. The library's generic `BIG MAX` and `BIG MIN` have no identity, so an empty one raises `EmptyReduction`. `tests/simpleSum` asserts it for `BIG MIN`; an empty `BIG MAX` raised under walk when measured (`reviews/flattening-questions-ways.md`, "Question 1", section 2). A reduction makes its identity at its own type (P-78). Detail: `reviews/max-min-identities-judgement.md` sections 1 and 2.
- F-61 **`perf-probes/prelude/REPORT.md` named three steps to making the interpreter's library the compiler's: the checker's sizes and the tower's errors are done.** The steps are: the checker checks `nat` and `int` static parameters (F-67); the library api's errors from the number and comparison tower are cleared (F-131); and the native bindings move to the compiled path's helpers (F-32). The report's run stopped in the library's apis, before the component, desugaring and code generation (section 5). The component's errors since are the distance, which also had to reach zero before the switch-over, and is 0 since climb batch 22 (F-53). No minimal `Array` or `Vector` added to the compiler's prelude can serve C4's `FlatArrays` (`run-c4/src/FlatArrays.fss`), which extends the library's array hierarchy and uses its whole protocol. Such a shim would reproduce `NativeArray.fss` and about 1,000 lines of the library above it. Detail: the same report, sections 5 (the steps) and 4 (the shim).
- F-62 **The tower closure, `AnyIntegral`'s `comprises` clause, checks as written on the compiled checker, under the specification's reading of `comprises`.** It builds P-44. The checker admits the unlisted `Integral[\I\]` by F-72's rule, which the specification states (F-171); the frozen 1.0 draft refuses it. Walk does not read the library's `comprises` clauses (rows 595, 596). The compiler library's `comprises I` idiom passes the checker and overflows walk's exclusion test (row 407). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-comprises-checker/REPORT.md` section 4.
- F-63 **The one library's api declares `String`'s `split` and `splitWithOffsets` once, abstract; redeclares no `zip` in `List`, where the inherited `ZeroIndexed.zip` serves; has `Condition.map` return `Condition[\G\]`, the component's type; and closes `QQ` by `comprises { ... }`.** `Condition` is the sequential generator trait at `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:934`. In their earlier forms, the pair declared twice and `List`'s `zip[\F\](other: List[\F\])`, the checker refused the api (measured). The other repairs tried, the plain pair kept once and a `zip` narrowed to `ZeroIndexed`, read the same count; the forms kept follow the specification's export rules (the report's Decisions). The `Condition.map` error was seen only under a checker change that did not land; otherwise it is read from the export check's comparison of return types, and no test gates that edit. `QQ`'s clause lists no type, since its one value type `Ratio` is private to the component, and an api may leave out a private type only by `...` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:400`). No api-declared type extends `QQ`, so F-64's refusal, which falls on such a type, does not arise. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-library-defects/REPORT.md`, "Summary", "Decisions" and "Defects and their homes".
